title: Effects and interaction of different interior material treatment and personal preference on psychological and physiological responses in living environment
research_question: To compare volunteers' physiological responses and subjective evaluations of wooden dwelling spaces with different wood materials (planed Japanese cedar lumber vs. printed grain resin sheet overlay boards) and to investigate the interaction with personal preference.

participants.description: 83 healthy adults (mean age±standard deviation: 37.1±14.7 years; 32 males, 51 females) from Kyushu University, Japan. None reported abnormal physical or mental health conditions.
participants.recruitment: Recruited for the study (details not specified beyond being healthy adults).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Two experimental rooms (Room A and Room B) of the same size (10 m² floor, 2.4 m ceiling, 24 m³ volume) and similar lighting conditions. Room A was finished with planed Japanese cedar lumber (floor, walls, ceiling). Room B was finished with printed grain resin sheet overlay boards (MDF with imitation wood-vinyl covering for floor, walls, ceiling). Foundation, pillars, crossbeams, and beams in both rooms were Japanese cedar lumber.

mechanisms: VOCs from solid natural wood can suppress SBP and SAA.
δ-cadinene influences physiological response and subjective evaluations, possibly via stimulation of parasympathetic nervous system (PSNS) activity.
Differences in VOCs concentrations influence subjective evaluations.
The presence of solid natural wood can relieve negative subjective mood status.
moderators: Personal preference (W group: wood preferred; L group: laminate preferred)
implementation_implications: Planed Japanese cedar lumber interiors can suppress negative mood changes more efficiently than artificial materials.
Physiological responses are important for validating subjective assessments of restorative properties of wood interiors.
Further research with controlled stressors and attention-depleting tasks is needed to verify restorative properties of wood interiors.

limitations: Despite efforts to make rooms visually similar, some subjects reported perceiving visual differences.
The effect of room-exposure order was not tested.
Insufficient detection and comparison of non-terpene VOCs, limiting understanding of artificial material VOC influence (e.g., glues).
No single compound was isolated for evaluation, preventing identification of specific compounds responsible for effects or their mechanisms.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractJapanese cedar (Cryptomeria japonica) wood is widely used as a traditional construction material in Japan. The relationship between an individual’s perceived comfort level and a preference for Japanese cedar wood interiors is of interest. We compared volunteers’ physiological responses and subjective evaluations of wooden dwelling spaces with different wood materials: planed Japanese cedar lumber, or printed grain resin sheet overlay boards. Eighty-three subjects were asked to stay in each room for 30 min. We evaluated salivary stress markers, blood pressure, the profile of mood states-brief form (POMS), and a questionnaire that used the semantic differential method to evaluate the subjects’ feeling state for both rooms. The concentrations of the volatile organic compounds in both rooms were also quantified after the experiment. The results demonstrated that the subjects’ evaluation of each room was highly dependent on their preference; each room was evaluated more positively by subjects who preferred it. Although the subjects’ feelings were also influenced by their preference, the room with Japanese cedar did not elicit negative feelings, even from the subjects who disliked it. The subjects’ physiological responses were totally independent of their preferences. Their blood pressure decreased in the Japanese cedar room, and their salivary alpha-amylase activity was repressed in both rooms. These results indicated that the subjective evaluations were influenced in part by the subjects’ preferences, while their physiological responses were not affected. Regardless of which room the subjects preferred, the Japanese cedar room reduced the subjects’ blood pressure compared to the room with artificial materials.
